questions.text: What sets this in an ordinary function?
options: The place where the function was declared
The call: the object before the dot, or call, apply, bind, or new
The value of the first local variable

questions.text: Why does const show = box.show; show() lose box?
options: A call without the dot does not pass box as this
Copying a method strips its body
box is deleted as soon as the method is copied
A method always has this === undefined

questions.text: Where does an arrow created inside a method get this?
options: From the object that owns the arrow
An arrow has no this of its own and takes it from the outer function
The arrow creates an empty object and uses that

questions.text: What does fn.bind(obj) return?
options: The result of calling fn immediately
The same fn with its body rewritten
A new function whose this is already fixed

questions.text: A method’s this is the object where the function was written, not the object it was called on.
An arrow written directly in an object literal gets that object as this.
box.show.bind(box) can be called on its own, and this stays box.
fn.call(obj) sets obj as this for that call.
Why does setTimeout(box.show, 0) lose the object box?
questions.answer: The timer calls the function itself, with no dot before the name. That call no longer passes box as this.

questions.text: Name two ways to keep this when a method has to be passed on.
questions.answer: Wrap the call: () => box.show(). Or bind it first: box.show.bind(box).

questions.text: What is this inside a function called with new?
questions.answer: The new object that new creates. Properties written to this end up on that object.

questions.text: Why do people write const self = this before a nested function?
questions.answer: An ordinary nested function gets its own this from its own call. self is a closed-over variable that keeps the outer method’s this.
